claim: The Rhynie chert is 407 million years old, dating to the Pragian–?earliest Emsian, Early Devonian period.
source: The 407-million-year-old, Pragian–?earliest Emsian, Early Devonian (Wellman, 2006) Rhynie chert fossil site provides a unique insight into the structure of plants during this key time in plant evolution.
evidence: The age and dating are supported by a citation to Wellman, 2006.

claim: The Rhynie chert preserves an entire Early Devonian hot spring ecosystem including plants, animals, fungi, and microbes in situ.
source: The Rhynie chert preserves an entire Early Devonian hot spring ecosystem, where plants, animals, fungi, and microbes are preserved in situ (Edwards et al., 2018; Garwood et al., 2020; Rice et al., 2002; Strullu-Derrien et al., 2019; Wellman, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: The Rhynie chert is the earliest time point in the fossil record where cellular details of rhizoid-based rooting systems, germinating spores, and fossilised meristems are preserved.
source: The exceptional preservation has been crucial for our understanding of early land plant evolution because it is the earliest time point in the fossil record where cellular details of rhizoid-based rooting systems, germinating spores, and fossilised meristems are preserved (Edwards, 2003; Hetherington and Dolan, 2018a; Hetherington and Dolan, 2018b; Kerp, 2018; Lyon, 1957; Taylor et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: Asteroxylon mackiei has been reconstructed as a plant that is approximately 30 cm high.
source: A. mackiei has been reconstructed as a plant that is approximately 30 cm high (Bhutta, 1969; Edwards, 2003), with highly branched shoot and rooting systems (Chaloner and MacDonald, 1980; Kerp, 2018; Kerp et al., 2013; Kidston and Lang, 1920; Kidston and Lang, 1921).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bhutta, 1969 and Edwards, 2003.

claim: Asteroxylon mackiei has highly branched shoot and rooting systems.
source: A. mackiei has been reconstructed as a plant that is approximately 30 cm high (Bhutta, 1969; Edwards, 2003), with highly branched shoot and rooting systems (Chaloner and MacDonald, 1980; Kerp, 2018; Kerp et al., 2013; Kidston and Lang, 1920; Kidston and Lang, 1921).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: Asteroxylon mackiei is a member of the earliest diverging lineage of the lycopsids, the Drepanophycales.
source: It holds an important phylogenetic position for understanding root and leaf evolution in lycophytes because it is a member of the earliest diverging lineage of the lycopsids, the Drepanophycales (Kenrick and Crane, 1997), and both the rooting axes and leaves of A. mackiei developed some but not all defining characteristics of roots and leaves in more derived species (Bower, 1908; Hetherington and Dolan, 2018a; Kenrick, 2002; Kidston and Lang, 1920).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kenrick and Crane, 1997.

claim: The rooting axes and leaves of Asteroxylon mackiei developed some but not all defining characteristics of roots and leaves in more derived species.
source: It holds an important phylogenetic position for understanding root and leaf evolution in lycophytes because it is a member of the earliest diverging lineage of the lycopsids, the Drepanophycales (Kenrick and Crane, 1997), and both the rooting axes and leaves of A. mackiei developed some but not all defining characteristics of roots and leaves in more derived species (Bower, 1908; Hetherington and Dolan, 2018a; Kenrick, 2002; Kidston and Lang, 1920).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: The drepanophycalean lycopsids are the earliest group of land plants in the fossil record with complex body plans comprising distinct rooting axes, root-bearing organs, and leafy shoots.
source: The drepanophycalean lycopsids are the earliest group of land plants in the fossil record with complex body plans comprising distinct rooting axes, root-bearing organs, and leafy shoots (Gensel et al., 2001; Gensel and Edwards, 2001; Hueber, 1992; Kenrick and Crane, 1997; Lang and Cookson, 1935; Matsunaga and Tomescu, 2016; Matsunaga and Tomescu, 2017; Stewart and Rothwell, 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: The evolution, radiation, and spread of drepanophycalean lycopsids across all continents contributed to the transformation of the terrestrial environment through their impact on soil formation and stabilisation, surface hydrology, and silicate weathering.
source: Their evolution, radiation, and spread across all continents contributed to the transformation of the terrestrial environment through their impact on soil formation and stabilisation, surface hydrology, and silicate weathering (Algeo and Scheckler, 1998; Gibling and Davies, 2012; Matsunaga and Tomescu, 2016; Xue et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: A 3D reconstruction of Asteroxylon mackiei was produced based on a series of 31 consecutive thick sections through a block of Rhynie chert.
source: To discover the structure and infer the development of the lycopsid A. mackiei, we produced a series of 31 consecutive thick sections through a block of Rhynie chert that preserved a branched network of connected A. mackiei axes in situ (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the methods described in the manuscript and references to figures showing the sections.

claim: The digitally reconstructed Asteroxylon mackiei plant occupied a volume of 4.8 cm in length, 3.5 cm in width, and 2.8 cm in height.
source: Using images of these thick sections, we digitally reconstructed the A. mackiei plant in a volume of 4.8 cm in length, 3.5 cm in width, and 2.8 cm in height (Figure 1A,B,G Video 1), which, to our knowledge, represents the largest evidence-based reconstruction for any Rhynie chert plant to date.
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements from the 3D reconstruction shown in Figure 1 and Video 1.

claim: The 3D reconstruction of Asteroxylon mackiei represents the largest evidence-based reconstruction for any Rhynie chert plant to date.
source: Using images of these thick sections, we digitally reconstructed the A. mackiei plant in a volume of 4.8 cm in length, 3.5 cm in width, and 2.8 cm in height (Figure 1A,B,G Video 1), which, to our knowledge, represents the largest evidence-based reconstruction for any Rhynie chert plant to date.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' knowledge of the literature and the size of their reconstruction.

claim: Three distinct axis types were distinguished in a single individual Asteroxylon mackiei plant: leafy shoot axes, root-bearing axes, and rooting axes.
source: We distinguished three distinct axis types in a single individual plant that we designate: leafy shoot axes, root-bearing axes, and rooting axes.
evidence: This claim is supported by observations from the 3D reconstruction and anatomical analysis.

claim: Leafy shoot axes of Asteroxylon mackiei developed leaves, abundant stomata, and a characteristic internal anatomy including a stellate xylem, many leaf traces, and trabecular zone.
source: Leafy shoot axes developed leaves, abundant stomata, and a characteristic internal anatomy including a stellate xylem, many leaf traces, and trabecular zone as reported for A. mackiei (Bhutta, 1969; Kerp, 2018; Kerp et al., 2013; Kidston and Lang, 1920; Kidston and Lang, 1921; Lyon, 1964; Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 1C,D and citations to previous descriptions.

claim: The main axis of Asteroxylon mackiei present in each thick section was horizontal (plagiotropic).
source: The main axis present in each of the thick sections was horizontal (plagiotropic) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations from the sections and geopetal evidence shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Four leafy shoot axes with similar anatomy attached to the main axis at anisotomous branch points in Asteroxylon mackiei.
source: Four leafy shoot axes with similar anatomy attached to the main axis at anisotomous branch points; an anisotomous branch point is a description of morphology and means that the diameters of the two axes connected at a branch point are different (Gola, 2014; Imaichi, 2008; Ollgaard, 1979; Yin and Meicenheimer, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations from the reconstruction and citations defining anisotomous branching.

claim: The diameter of the main plagiotropic leafy shoot of Asteroxylon mackiei was approximately 1 cm.
source: The diameter of the main plagiotropic leafy shoot was ca. 1 cm and the thinner leafy shoots attached at branch points were ca. 0.6 cm.
evidence: This claim is based on measurements from the fossil specimens.

claim: The thinner leafy shoots attached at branch points in Asteroxylon mackiei were approximately 0.6 cm in diameter.
source: The diameter of the main plagiotropic leafy shoot was ca. 1 cm and the thinner leafy shoots attached at branch points were ca. 0.6 cm.
evidence: This claim is based on measurements from the fossil specimens.

claim: Some of the thinner leafy shoots in Asteroxylon mackiei were orientated closer to the vertical, indicating orthotropic growth orientation.
source: Some of the thinner leafy shoots were orientated closer to the vertical, indicating orthotropic growth orientation (Figure 1A,B,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations from the 3D reconstruction shown in Figure 1.

claim: The xylem was less lobed in plagiotropic leafy shoots of Asteroxylon mackiei than in orthotropic leafy shoot axes.
source: The most noticeable differences between the plagiotropic leafy shoots described here and orthotropic shoots described previously (Bhutta, 1969; Kerp et al., 2013; Kidston and Lang, 1920; Kidston and Lang, 1921; Lyon, 1964) are that the xylem was less lobed and there were fewer leaf traces in the plagiotropic leafy shoot axes than in the orthotropic leafy shoot axes (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical observations shown in Figure 1D and comparison with previous descriptions.

claim: There were fewer leaf traces in plagiotropic leafy shoot axes of Asteroxylon mackiei than in orthotropic leafy shoot axes.
source: The most noticeable differences between the plagiotropic leafy shoots described here and orthotropic shoots described previously (Bhutta, 1969; Kerp et al., 2013; Kidston and Lang, 1920; Kidston and Lang, 1921; Lyon, 1964) are that the xylem was less lobed and there were fewer leaf traces in the plagiotropic leafy shoot axes than in the orthotropic leafy shoot axes (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical observations shown in Figure 1D and comparison with previous descriptions.

claim: Fewer leaf traces in plagiotropic regions of Asteroxylon mackiei is consistent with a lower leaf density on these axes than in orthotropic axes.
source: Fewer leaf traces in plagiotropic regions is consistent with a lower leaf density on these axes than in orthotropic axes, a feature demonstrated in detail by the discovery of an isolated plagiotropic leafy shoot with sparse covering of leaves preserved on the exterior of a block of chert (Figure 1H,J).
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from anatomical observations and direct observation of a specimen shown in Figure 1H,J.

claim: Root-bearing axes of Asteroxylon mackiei were attached to leafy shoot axes at anisotomous branch points.
source: Root-bearing axes of A. mackiei were attached to leafy shoot axes at anisotomous branch points, where the thinner daughter axis developed as a root-bearing axis and the thicker daughter axis developed as a leafy shoot axis (Figures 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations from the reconstruction shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Diameters of root-bearing axes in Asteroxylon mackiei were approximately 0.35 cm compared to leafy shoot axes typically over 0.6 cm.
source: Diameters of root-bearing axes were ca. 0.35 cm compared to leafy shoots axes typically over 0.6 cm.
evidence: This claim is based on measurements from the fossil specimens.

claim: In Asteroxylon mackiei, root-bearing axes attached to first-order leafy shoot axes close to where the latter attached to the main shoot.
source: In the four other examples (Figure 2D–I), root-bearing axes were attached to side branches of the main leafy shoot. These branches were termed first-order leafy shoots because they were separated from the main shoot by a single branching event. Root-bearing axes attached to first-order leafy shoot axes close to where the latter attached to the main shoot.
evidence: This claim is supported by observations from the reconstruction shown in Figure 2D-I.

claim: The branch arrangement where two adjacent anisotomous branches originate close to each other is termed k-branching.
source: The branch arrangement where two adjacent anisotomous branches originate close to each other is termed k-branching (Chomicki et al., 2017; Edwards, 1994; Gensel et al., 2001; Gensel and Berry, 2001; Gerrienne, 1988; Matsunaga and Tomescu, 2016; Matsunaga and Tomescu, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations defining the term k-branching.

claim: The root-bearing axes of Sengelia radicans are attached to leafy shoot axes at k-branch points.
source: The root-bearing axes of the Drepanophycalean lycopsid Sengelia radicans (Matsunaga and Tomescu, 2016; Matsunaga and Tomescu, 2017) are attached to leafy shoot axes at k-branch points.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research on Sengelia radicans.

claim: In both Asteroxylon mackiei and Sengelia radicans, root-bearing axes developed an epidermis and cuticle with occasional stomata and scale leaves.
source: In both A. mackiei and S. radicans, root-bearing axes developed an epidermis and cuticle with occasional stomata and scale leaves.
evidence: This claim is based on observations from A. mackiei and comparison with published descriptions of S. radicans.

claim: In the root-bearing axes of Asteroxylon mackiei where anatomy could be investigated, the xylem strand was elliptical, not lobed as in leafy shoot axes.
source: In the root-bearing axes of A. mackiei where anatomy could be investigated the xylem strand was elliptical, not lobed as in leafy shoot axes, and there were few or no leaf traces, which distinguishes them from leafy shoots in which leaf traces were abundant (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical observations shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Root-bearing axes of Asteroxylon mackiei had few or no leaf traces, which distinguishes them from leafy shoots in which leaf traces were abundant.
source: In the root-bearing axes of A. mackiei where anatomy could be investigated the xylem strand was elliptical, not lobed as in leafy shoot axes, and there were few or no leaf traces, which distinguishes them from leafy shoots in which leaf traces were abundant (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical observations shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Root-bearing axes in Asteroxylon mackiei were a distinct axis type and not merely a transitional zone between two axis types.
source: These differences in anatomy and morphology between root-bearing axes and leafy shoots demonstrate that root-bearing axes were a distinct axis type and not merely a transitional zone between two axis types as previously suggested (Bhutta, 1969; Kidston and Lang, 1920; Kidston and Lang, 1921).
evidence: This claim is based on anatomical and morphological observations that contradict previous interpretations.

claim: An isolated bifurcating axis with two apices was discovered that represents the apex of a root-bearing axis in Asteroxylon mackiei.
source: We searched for apices on axes with the characters of root-bearing axes and discovered an isolated bifurcating axis with two apices (Figure 2J,K).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations of a specimen shown in Figure 2J,K.

claim: The apices of the bifurcating axis were assigned to Asteroxylon mackiei because of the presence of leaves on the parent axis and a small leaf on the flank of the upper apex.
source: The apices were assigned to A. mackiei because of the presence of leaves on the parent axis (Figure 2J, arrowheads) and a small leaf on the flank of the upper apex (Figure 2J,K), A. mackiei is the only Rhynie chert plant with leaves.
evidence: This claim is based on the presence of leaves, which are unique to A. mackiei among Rhynie chert plants.

claim: Asteroxylon mackiei is the only Rhynie chert plant with leaves.
source: The apices were assigned to A. mackiei because of the presence of leaves on the parent axis (Figure 2J, arrowheads) and a small leaf on the flank of the upper apex (Figure 2J,K), A. mackiei is the only Rhynie chert plant with leaves.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of Rhynie chert plants.

claim: Both apices of the root-bearing axis were covered by an unbroken cuticle.
source: Both apices were covered by an unbroken cuticle, and a single small leaf was present on the upper apex, which together demonstrate that these are apices of root-bearing axes and not apices of rooting axes that lack leaves and cuticles (Hetherington and Dolan, 2018a), or leafy shoots where the apex is covered by a large number of leaves (Edwards, 2003; Hueber, 1992; Kerp, 2018; Kerp et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations of the specimen and comparison with other axis types.

claim: Rooting axes of Asteroxylon mackiei were always less than 2 mm in diameter and frequently less than 1 mm.
source: Rooting axes were always less than 2 mm in diameter and frequently less than 1 mm and were highly branched (Bhutta, 1969; Hetherington and Dolan, 2018a; Kidston and Lang, 1920; Kidston and Lang, 1921).
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements from specimens and citations to previous descriptions.

claim: Rooting axes of Asteroxylon mackiei were highly branched.
source: Rooting axes were always less than 2 mm in diameter and frequently less than 1 mm and were highly branched (Bhutta, 1969; Hetherington and Dolan, 2018a; Kidston and Lang, 1920; Kidston and Lang, 1921).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations from specimens and citations to previous descriptions.

claim: Leaves, leaf traces, stomata, and cuticles were never found on rooting axes of Asteroxylon mackiei, even when the epidermis was well preserved.
source: Leaves, leaf traces, stomata, and cuticles were never found on rooting axes, even when the epidermis was well preserved (Kidston and Lang, 1920).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations from specimens and a citation to previous descriptions.

claim: The epidermis of rooting axes in Asteroxylon mackiei was frequently missing, suggesting that it was lost in older axes.
source: The epidermis was frequently missing, suggesting that it was lost in older axes and the outer cortex was often limited to one or two cell layers (Figure 1F; Kidston and Lang, 1920).
evidence: This claim is based on observations from specimens and inference about the developmental state of the axes.

claim: A single well-preserved highly branched rooting axis was found attached to a root-bearing axis at an anisotomous branch point in the reconstruction of Asteroxylon mackiei.
source: We found a single well-preserved highly branched rooting axis in our reconstruction (Figure 3A–F). This rooting axis was attached to a root-bearing axis at an anisotomous branch point (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations from the reconstruction shown in Figure 3.

claim: The rooting axis of Asteroxylon mackiei had a circular xylem strand at the centre.
source: There was a circular xylem strand at the centre of the rooting axis.
evidence: This claim is based on anatomical observations from the reconstruction.

claim: The diameter of the rooting axis of Asteroxylon mackiei where it attached to the root-bearing axis was approximately 2 mm but decreased in size distally at successive branch points.
source: The diameter of the rooting axis where it attached to the root-bearing axis was ca. 2 mm but decreased in size distally at successive branch points.
evidence: This claim is based on measurements from the reconstruction.

claim: The rooting axis of Asteroxylon mackiei was weakly gravitropic in contrast to the strong gravitropic growth observed in root-bearing axes.
source: The rooting axis was weakly gravitropic in contrast to the strong gravitropic growth observed in root-bearing axes (Figure 3A,E).
evidence: This claim is based on observations of growth orientation from the reconstruction shown in Figure 3.

claim: The rooting axis of Asteroxylon mackiei showed over four orders of branching preserved in less than 1 cm in the reconstruction.
source: The profuse branching of the rooting axis is evident with over four orders of branching preserved in less than 1 cm in our reconstruction (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations from the reconstruction shown in Figure 3E.

claim: No evidence was found that other axis types developed from the rooting axis in Asteroxylon mackiei.
source: We found no evidence that other axis types developed from the rooting axis.
evidence: This claim is based on the absence of observations in the reconstruction.

claim: The morphological and anatomical boundary between the root-bearing axis and rooting axis in Asteroxylon mackiei was clear and defined at the point of branching.
source: The morphological and anatomical boundary between the root-bearing axis and rooting axis was clear (Figure 3C); it involved the change from strong gravitropic growth to weak gravitropic growth, and the absence of scale leaves, stomata, and a well-marked cuticle all found on root-bearing axes but absent on rooting axes. This suggests that the boundary between the two axis types is defined at the point of branching and not in a continuum along a single axis.
evidence: This claim is based on observations from the reconstruction and inference about developmental boundaries.

claim: The rooting axes of Asteroxylon mackiei were transitional between the ancestral rootless state and the derived state characterised by true roots with caps as found in extant lycopsids.
source: The rooting axes of A. mackiei hold a key position for interpreting the origin of roots in lycopsids because they were transitional between the ancestral rootless state and the derived state characterised by true roots with caps as found in extant lycopsids (Hetherington and Dolan, 2018a; Hetherington and Dolan, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on the evolutionary position of A. mackiei rooting axes.

claim: A number of characters are shared between the rooting axes of Asteroxylon mackiei and rooting axes of other members of the Drepanophycales, including their attachment to root-bearing axes, weak gravitropic growth, and profuse dichotomous branching.
source: Our reconstruction demonstrates that a number of characters are shared between the rooting axes of A. mackiei and rooting axes of other members of the Drepanophycales, including their attachment to root-bearing axes, weak gravitropic growth, and profuse dichotomous branching.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of observations from A. mackiei with published descriptions of other Drepanophycales.

claim: Rooting axes in Asteroxylon mackiei connected to root-bearing axes at anisotomous branch points.
source: Our new reconstruction indicates that rooting axes connected to root-bearing axes at anisotomous branch points.
evidence: This claim is supported by observations from the 3D reconstruction.

claim: There are two modes of branching that could produce anisotomous branch point morphology in extant lycopsids: endogenous branching or dichotomous branching.
source: Based on development of extant lycopsids (Bierhorst, 1971; Fujinami et al., 2021; Gola, 2014; Guttenberg, 1966; Harrison et al., 2007; Hetherington and Dolan, 2017; Imaichi, 2008; Imaichi and Kato, 1989; Ogura, 1972; Ollgaard, 1979; Spencer et al., 2021; Yi and Kato, 2001; Yin and Meicenheimer, 2017), there are two modes of branching that could produce anisotomous branch point morphology, endogenous branching, or dichotomous branching.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to research on lycopsid development.

claim: Endogenous branching is the mode of branching where the meristem of the new axis develops from the internal tissues of the parent axis and breaks through the parent tissue to emerge.
source: Endogenous branching is the mode of branching where the meristem of the new axis develops from the internal tissues of the parent axis and breaks through the parent tissue to emerge, a mode of development typical of the initiation of roots of extant lycopsid species.
evidence: This claim is a definition supported by established knowledge of plant development.

claim: Dichotomous branching is the mode of branching where the parent meristem splits in two to produce two daughter axes.
source: Dichotomous branching is the mode of branching where the parent meristem splits in two to produce two daughter axes, a mode of development typical of roots, shoots, and rhizophores in extant lycopsids (Bierhorst, 1971; Bruchmann, 1874; Gola, 2014; Guttenberg, 1966; Harrison et al., 2007; Hetherington and Dolan, 2017; Imaichi, 2008; Imaichi and Kato, 1989; Ogura, 1972; Ollgaard, 1979; Spencer et al., 2021; Wigglesworth, 1907; Yi and Kato, 2001; Yin and Meicenheimer, 2017).
evidence: This claim is a definition supported by multiple citations to research on lycopsid development.

claim: A 3D reconstruction of an anisotomous branch point connecting a root-bearing axis and rooting axis in Asteroxylon mackiei was produced based on 119 peels.
source: We produced a 3D reconstruction of the anisotomous branch point that connects the two axes based on 119 peels (Figure 4, Video 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the methods described and the reconstruction shown in Figure 4 and Video 2.

claim: Tissues were continuous between the root-bearing axis and rooting axis in Asteroxylon mackiei.
source: Tissues were continuous between the root-bearing axis and rooting axis.
evidence: This claim is supported by observations from the 3D reconstruction of the branch point.

claim: The vascular trace for the rooting axis in Asteroxylon mackiei was seen to branch off and then run parallel to the main vascular trace before gradually arcing into the rooting axis.
source: The vascular trace for the rooting axis was seen to branch off and then run parallel to the main vascular trace before gradually arcing into the rooting axis (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations from the 3D reconstruction shown in Figure 4.

claim: The dichotomy of the vascular trace suggests that rooting axes in Asteroxylon mackiei developed from root-bearing axes by dichotomous branching.
source: These characteristics, especially the dichotomy of the vascular trace, suggest that rooting axes developed from root-bearing axes by dichotomous branching.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from anatomical observations of the vascular trace.

claim: Two fossilised Asteroxylon mackiei meristems were identified on a single thin section.
source: We identified two fossilised A. mackiei meristems on a single thin section.
evidence: This claim is supported by observations from a thin section specimen.

claim: The thin section preserves a large Asteroxylon mackiei leafy shoot axis approximately 5 mm in diameter with stellate xylem cut in transverse section.
source: This thin section preserves a large A. mackiei leafy shoot axis ca. 5 mm in diameter with stellate xylem cut in transverse section at the top of the image (Figure 5A, green arrowhead).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations from the thin section shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Attached to the leafy shoot axis is a smaller root-bearing axis approximately 1.9 mm in diameter close to the attachment with the leafy shoot.
source: Attached to the leafy shoot axis is a smaller root-bearing axis ca. 1.9 mm in diameter close to the attachment with the leafy shoot.
evidence: This claim is based on measurements from the thin section specimen.

claim: The two apices on either side of the root-bearing axis are interpreted as meristems of rooting axes based on their domed structure and the large number of small cells close to the apices.
source: Close to the base of the thin section are two apices on either side of the root-bearing axis (Figure 5A, white arrowheads). We interpret these as meristems because of their domed structure and the large number of small cells close to the apices. Given the attachment of these meristems to root-bearing axes and their small size, we interpret them as meristems of rooting axes.
evidence: This claim is based on morphological observations and inference about the identity of the structures.

claim: Cell files are continuous between the root-bearing axes and rooting axes in Asteroxylon mackiei.
source: Cell files are continuous between the root-bearing axes and rooting axes, and there is no evidence that the rooting axes initiated by endogenous branching and broke through the ground or dermal tissues of the root-bearing axes.
evidence: This claim is supported by observations from the thin section specimen.

claim: There is no evidence that the rooting axes in Asteroxylon mackiei initiated by endogenous branching and broke through the ground or dermal tissues of the root-bearing axes.
source: Cell files are continuous between the root-bearing axes and rooting axes, and there is no evidence that the rooting axes initiated by endogenous branching and broke through the ground or dermal tissues of the root-bearing axes.
evidence: This claim is based on the absence of evidence for endogenous branching in the specimens.

claim: The organisation of cells in the meristems is consistent with the hypothesis that rooting axes in Asteroxylon mackiei developed by dichotomous branching from root-bearing axes.
source: The organisation of cells in these meristems is consistent with our hypothesis based on 3D reconstructed anatomy that the rooting axes developed by dichotomous branching from root-bearing axes.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from cellular observations supporting the dichotomous branching hypothesis.

claim: Rooting axes in Asteroxylon mackiei originated by dichotomous branching.
source: We discovered that A. mackiei rooting axes originate by dichotomous branching.
evidence: This claim is the main conclusion based on anatomical and developmental evidence presented in the manuscript.

claim: The branch connecting rooting axes and root-bearing axes in Asteroxylon mackiei was always anisotomous.
source: Furthermore, the branch connecting rooting axes and root-bearing axes was always anisotomous.
evidence: This claim is based on observations from all examined specimens.

claim: Roots do not originate by dichotomy in extant lycopsids.
source: This finding is significant because roots do not originate by dichotomy in extant lycopsids.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of extant lycopsid development.

claim: Roots of extant lycopsids originate endogenously from shoots, rhizophores, and rhizomorphs.
source: Instead, roots of extant lycopsids originate endogenously from shoots, rhizophores, and rhizomorphs (Bruchmann, 1874; Guttenberg, 1966; Hetherington and Dolan, 2017; Imaichi, 2008; Imaichi and Kato, 1989; Ogura, 1972; Yi and Kato, 2001), and in rare cases by exogenous development in embryos, protocorms, or tubers where dichotomous branching does not occur (Bower, 1908; Hetherington and Dolan, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to research on extant lycopsid development.

claim: The origin of Asteroxylon mackiei rooting axes by anisotomous dichotomy was different from the origin of roots in extant lycopsids, and this developmental mechanism is now extinct.
source: The origin of A. mackiei rooting axes by anisotomous dichotomy was therefore different from the origin of roots in extant lycopsids, and this developmental mechanism is now extinct (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of A. mackiei development with extant lycopsids and inference about evolutionary history.

claim: Dichotomous branching, where the daughter axes produced at a branch point were of different types, was a characteristic of the rooting system of Asteroxylon mackiei.
source: These reconstructions highlight that dichotomous branching, where the daughter axes produced at a branch point were of different types, was a characteristic of the rooting system of A. mackiei.
evidence: This claim is based on observations from the 3D reconstructions.

claim: Nothia aphylla is an extinct early lycophyte closely related to the lycopsids.
source: Nothia aphylla is an extinct early lycophyte closely related to the lycopsids (Kenrick and Crane, 1997; Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to phylogenetic research.

claim: The rooting system of Nothia aphylla consisted of horizontal (plagiotropic) sporophyte axes with rhizoids that were both morphologically and anatomically different from the vertical (orthotropic) shoot axes.
source: Its rooting system consisted of horizontal (plagiotropic) sporophyte axes with rhizoids, called rhizoidal sporophyte axes, that were both morphologically and anatomically different from the vertical (orthotropic) shoot axes (Hetherington and Dolan, 2018b; Kerp et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research on N. aphylla.

claim: The plagiotropic axes of Nothia aphylla attach to the base of orthotropic axes at branch points.
source: The plagiotropic axes attach to the base of orthotropic axes at branch points (Kerp et al., 2001), suggesting that the transitions between orthotropic and plagiotropic growth occurred at branch points.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research on N. aphylla.

claim: Axis type could change at branch points in Nothia aphylla as it does in Asteroxylon mackiei.
source: This demonstrates that axis type could change at branch points in N. aphylla as it does in A. mackiei.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from observations of both species.

claim: Change in axis type at branch points was a characteristic of the rooting systems of the zosterophylls.
source: Change in axis type at branch points was also a characteristic of the rooting systems of the zosterophylls, the other major grouping of extinct lycophytes.
evidence: This claim is based on observations from multiple zosterophyll species described in the manuscript.

claim: Zosterophylls are a paraphyletic or polyphyletic grouping of early-diverging lycophytes; however, most species group into a single clade sister to lycopsids.
source: Zosterophylls are a paraphyletic or polyphyletic grouping of early-diverging lycophytes; however, most species group into a single clade sister to lycopsids (Kenrick and Crane, 1997; Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to phylogenetic research.

claim: Many zosterophylls developed extensive rooting systems both morphologically and anatomically different from their shoot systems.
source: Many zosterophylls developed extensive rooting systems both morphologically and anatomically different from their shoot systems (Edwards, 2003; Gensel et al., 2001; Hao et al., 2010; Hao et al., 2007; Kotyk and Basinger, 2000; Li, 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published research on zosterophylls.

claim: In the zosterophyll Bathurstia denticulate, rooting axes formed at k-branching points on shoot axes.
source: In the zosterophyll Bathurstia denticulate (Gensel et al., 2001; Kotyk and Basinger, 2000), rooting axes formed at k-branching points on shoot axes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research on Bathurstia denticulate.

claim: The body plan of Asteroxylon mackiei was similar to the cosmopolitan members of the Drepanophycales found across America, Europe, and China in the Early and Middle Devonian.
source: We draw three significant conclusions from our 3D reconstruction of A. mackiei. (1) The body plan of A. mackiei was similar to the cosmopolitan members of the Drepanophycales found across America, Europe, and China in the Early and Middle Devonian (Gensel et al., 2001; Li and Edwards, 1995; Matsunaga and Tomescu, 2016; Matsunaga and Tomescu, 2017; Rayner, 1984; Schweitzer, 1980; Schweitzer and Giesen, 1980; Xu et al., 2013; Xue et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of A. mackiei with other Drepanophycales and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Mechanisms of body plan construction in Asteroxylon mackiei likely also operated in other Devonian Drepanophycales.
source: This suggests that despite inhabiting the Rhynie geothermal wetland ecosystem (Edwards et al., 2018; Garwood et al., 2020; Rice et al., 2002; Strullu-Derrien et al., 2019; Wellman, 2018), mechanisms of body plan construction in A. mackiei likely also operated in other Devonian Drepanophycales.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the similarity of body plans across Drepanophycales.

claim: In extant lycopsids, roots originate endogenously from shoots or specialised root producing structures, such as rhizophores.
source: In extant lycopsids, roots originate endogenously from shoots or specialised root producing structures, such as rhizophores (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of extant lycopsid development.

claim: Once developed, roots, shoots, and rhizophores in extant lycopsids branch dichotomously.
source: Once developed, roots, shoots, and rhizophores branch dichotomously (Chomicki et al., 2017; Fujinami et al., 2021; Gola, 2014; Harrison et al., 2007; Hetherington and Dolan, 2017; Imaichi, 2008; Imaichi and Kato, 1991; Ollgaard, 1979; Yin and Meicenheimer, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to research on extant lycopsid development.

claim: In extant lycopsids, the two daughter axes produced by dichotomous branching are always identical to the original axis.
source: However, the two daughter axes produced by dichotomous branching are always identical to the original axis: a shoot axis may branch dichotomously to form two identical shoot axes, a root axis may branch to form two identical root axes, and a rhizophore branches to form two identical rhizophores (Chomicki et al., 2017; Fujinami et al., 2021; Gola, 2014; Harrison et al., 2007; Hetherington and Dolan, 2017; Imaichi, 2008; Imaichi and Kato, 1991; Ollgaard, 1979; Yin and Meicenheimer, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to research on extant lycopsid development.

claim: In Asteroxylon mackiei, the root-bearing axes branched anisotomously to produce one root-bearing axis and a rooting axis.
source: In A. mackiei, the root-bearing axes branched anisotomously to produce one root-bearing axis and a rooting axis.
evidence: This claim is based on observations from the 3D reconstructions.

claim: Anisotomous dichotomy was key for the development of the complex body plan of Asteroxylon mackiei.
source: Our findings therefore suggest that anisotomous dichotomy was key for the development of the complex body plan of A. mackiei, which builds on previous suggestions that the evolution of anisotomous dichotomy in land plants was a key developmental innovation for both the evolution of leaves (Sanders et al., 2007; Stewart and Rothwell, 1993; Zimmerman, 1952) and rooting systems (Gensel et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from observations and supported by citations to previous hypotheses.

claim: The evolution of anisotomous dichotomy in land plants was a key developmental innovation for the evolution of leaves.
source: Our findings therefore suggest that anisotomous dichotomy was key for the development of the complex body plan of A. mackiei, which builds on previous suggestions that the evolution of anisotomous dichotomy in land plants was a key developmental innovation for both the evolution of leaves (Sanders et al., 2007; Stewart and Rothwell, 1993; Zimmerman, 1952) and rooting systems (Gensel et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research proposing this hypothesis.

claim: The evolution of anisotomous dichotomy in land plants was a key developmental innovation for the evolution of rooting systems.
source: Our findings therefore suggest that anisotomous dichotomy was key for the development of the complex body plan of A. mackiei, which builds on previous suggestions that the evolution of anisotomous dichotomy in land plants was a key developmental innovation for both the evolution of leaves (Sanders et al., 2007; Stewart and Rothwell, 1993; Zimmerman, 1952) and rooting systems (Gensel et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research proposing this hypothesis.

claim: The body plan of Asteroxylon mackiei comprised three distinct axis types.
source: Taken together, our 3D reconstruction demonstrates that the body plan of A. mackiei comprised three distinct axis types, and we demonstrate that roots developed through anisotomous dichotomy of a specialised root-bearing axis.
evidence: This claim is a summary conclusion based on the 3D reconstruction data.

claim: Roots in Asteroxylon mackiei developed through anisotomous dichotomy of a specialised root-bearing axis.
source: Taken together, our 3D reconstruction demonstrates that the body plan of A. mackiei comprised three distinct axis types, and we demonstrate that roots developed through anisotomous dichotomy of a specialised root-bearing axis.
evidence: This claim is a summary conclusion based on anatomical and developmental evidence.

claim: The mode of rooting system development by anisotomous dichotomy is now extinct.
source: This mode of rooting system development is now extinct, but played a key role in the development of the complex rooting systems of the Drepanophycales.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison with extant lycopsids and inference about evolutionary history.

claim: Anisotomous dichotomy played a key role in the development of the complex rooting systems of the Drepanophycales.
source: This mode of rooting system development is now extinct, but played a key role in the development of the complex rooting systems of the Drepanophycales.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from observations of A. mackiei and comparison with other Drepanophycales.

claim: The reconstruction of Asteroxylon mackiei was based on thick sections made from a single block of chert collected from a trench dug in 1964.
source: The reconstruction of A. mackiei was based on a series of 31 thick sections made from a single block of chert collected from a trench dug in 1964.
evidence: This claim describes the materials used in the study.

claim: Thick sections were deposited in the collection of the Forschungsstelle für Geologie und Paläontologie, Westfälische Wilhelms-Universität, Münster, Germany, under the accession numbers Pb 4161–4191.
source: Thick sections were not sealed with a cover slip and were deposited in the collection of the Forschungsstelle für Geologie und Paläontologie, Westfälische Wilhelms-Universität, Münster, Germany, under the accession numbers Pb 4161–4191.
evidence: This claim provides information about specimen deposition.

claim: Images of the full series of thick sections were deposited on Zenodo.
source: Images of the full series of thick sections were deposited on Zenodo (http://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.4287297).
evidence: This claim provides information about data availability.

claim: The 3D reconstruction was deposited on Zenodo.
source: Images and animations of the reconstruction were made in Blender, and the 3D reconstruction was deposited on Zenodo (http://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.4287297).
evidence: This claim provides information about data availability.

claim: A branching root-bearing axis was reconstructed from a series of RCA 1–119 from the A. Bhutta collection at the University of Cardiff.
source: A branching root-bearing axis was reconstructed from a series of RCA 1–119 from the A. Bhutta collection (Bhutta, 1969) at the University of Cardiff.
evidence: This claim describes the materials used for a specific reconstruction.

claim: The Asteroxylon mackiei rooting axis developed from root-bearing axes by anisotomous dichotomy.
source: Combining this reconstruction with developmental data from fossilised meristems, we demonstrate that the A. mackiei rooting axis – a transitional lycophyte organ between the rootless ancestral state and true roots – developed from root-bearing axes by anisotomous dichotomy.
evidence: This is a main finding of the study based on 3D reconstruction and developmental data.

claim: The Asteroxylon mackiei rooting axis is a transitional lycophyte organ between the rootless ancestral state and true roots.
source: Combining this reconstruction with developmental data from fossilised meristems, we demonstrate that the A. mackiei rooting axis – a transitional lycophyte organ between the rootless ancestral state and true roots – developed from root-bearing axes by anisotomous dichotomy.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of A. mackiei with ancestral and derived lycophytes.

claim: The Silurian–Devonian terrestrial revolution saw the evolution of vascular plants with complex bodies comprising distinct roots, root-bearing organs, shoots, and leaves from morphologically simpler ancestors.
source: The Silurian–Devonian terrestrial revolution saw the evolution of vascular plants with complex bodies comprising distinct roots, root-bearing organs, shoots, and leaves from morphologically simpler ancestors characterised by networks of undifferentiated axes (Bateman et al., 1998; Gensel and Edwards, 2001; Kenrick and Crane, 1997; Stewart and Rothwell, 1993; Xue et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published research on early plant evolution.

claim: Morphologically simpler ancestors of vascular plants were characterised by networks of undifferentiated axes.
source: The Silurian–Devonian terrestrial revolution saw the evolution of vascular plants with complex bodies comprising distinct roots, root-bearing organs, shoots, and leaves from morphologically simpler ancestors characterised by networks of undifferentiated axes (Bateman et al., 1998; Gensel and Edwards, 2001; Kenrick and Crane, 1997; Stewart and Rothwell, 1993; Xue et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published research on early plant evolution.
